ch58.anchor: the office of rikugun-bugyō-nami, Assistant Commissioner of the Army
ch58.note: Rikugun-bugyō-nami, “associate Army Commissioner,” was a genuine rank in the late-Tokugawa military hierarchy: the deputy grade of the rikugun-bugyō who oversaw the shogunate’s Western-style army. Toshizō’s firmly documented appointment to this office came a little later, in the Ezo (Hakodate) government of the winter of 1868, where he served under Ōtori as effective vice-minister of the army. Shiba brings the title forward to the Sendai phase; the exact dating here is the novel’s, but the office itself is real.

ch58.anchor: as head of the Ōshū alliance
ch58.note: The Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, the league of the domains of Mutsu (Ōshū), Dewa, and Echigo, was formed in the summer of 1868 to resist the new government and shield Aizu. Sendai, its largest member, was the keystone; when Sendai wavered and then submitted in the ninth month, as this chapter shows, the league fell apart, and with it the last hope of a stand on the main island.

Date Masamune (1567–1636), known by his posthumous honorific as Lord Teizan, was the one-eyed warlord who founded the Sendai domain and built its castle at Aoba. The Date house he left was, at 625,000 koku, among the greatest in Japan. Toshizō appeals to the memory of its martial founder to shame the present lord toward war.

ch58.anchor: the artillery officer Brunet, the artillery sergeant Fortant
ch58.note: Jules Brunet (1838–1911) was a French artillery officer of the military mission that had drilled the shogunal army. When France recalled the mission, Brunet resigned his commission and stayed on to fight beside the shogunal remnant, following Enomoto and Hijikata north to Hakodate: the foreign officer who cast his lot with the losing side, and, much later, one of the historical inspirations for the film The Last Samurai.

ch58.anchor: a Shimizu no Jirōchō or a Kunisada Chūji might have said
ch58.note: Shimizu no Jirōchō (1820–1893) and Kunisada Chūji (1810–1851) were famous bakuto, gambler-bosses of the late-Edo underworld whose exploits filled the popular storytellers’ repertoire. To say that Toshizō’s stump-speech sounded like theirs is to set his blunt, plain-man’s eloquence a world below the polished statecraft the moment demanded — the narrator’s affectionate needle.

ch58.anchor: he passed for a brilliant scholar even at the Shōheikō
ch58.note: The Shōheikō (the Shōheizaka Gakumonjo) was the shogunate’s official academy in Edo, the seat of orthodox Confucian learning and the training-ground of its scholar-officials; the modern University of Tokyo counts it among its forerunners, as the next line notes. That the unlettered Toshizō had once bested one of its star pupils sword in hand is just what gives Ōtori’s jab its edge.
